cultivar: Assam-type bushes in some gardens, hill-type bushes in others; not well documented
processing: Small-batch orthodox black tea, hand-plucked, with a long wither, gentle rolling and fairly light oxidation in spring, fuller later in the year; the same gardens make a little green and white tea.
harvest_season: March to November; spring and autumn pickings are best, summer leaf is bolder.
appearance_dry: Twisted leaf in brown, olive and gold.
taste_profile: Floral, lightly muscatel and honeyed, close in style to a good Darjeeling or Nepal tea, with a smooth, mid-weight body.

brewing.notes: Brew like a hill tea: around 90 °C, no milk, a second steep.

vintage_note: Made by a handful of small gardens (Lakyrsiew near Shillong is the best known) and sold by flush and year in small lots through speciality retailers in India and a few importers abroad; some leaf also goes unnamed to the Guwahati auction. Buy the current year's spring or autumn lot and drink within a year or two.
description:
Meghalaya, the wet, hilly state south of Assam, has grown tea only on a small scale and mostly in recent decades, but a few gardens in the Khasi and Ri-Bhoi hills have shown that the altitude and Darjeeling-type bushes can give something closer to Darjeeling or Nepal than to the Assam plains below. Lakyrsiew, a small garden near Shillong, is the name most drinkers meet.

The teas are hand-plucked and made in small orthodox batches: a long wither, gentle rolling, fairly light oxidation for the spring lots and fuller oxidation later in the year. The same gardens make small amounts of green and white tea.

The cup is bright amber and floral with a hint of muscatel and honey, smooth and mid-weight, with a clean, brisk finish. Brew it like a hill tea, around 90 °C for three to four minutes, without milk, and give it a second steep.

It is sold by flush and year in small lots, mostly through speciality retailers in India and a few importers abroad; some leaf also goes to the Guwahati auction as unnamed Meghalaya tea. Spring and autumn lots are the ones to look for, and the tea should be drunk within a year or two.

A genuine rarity rather than a marketing one: if you see a named Meghalaya garden on a list, it is worth a sample for the comparison with Darjeeling alone.
sources_note: Garden details (Lakyrsiew planting date and location) from memory; Meghalaya tea has no Wikipedia article, so 'Black tea' is used as umbrella.
history:
Tea in Meghalaya is mostly a story of recent decades. A growers' cooperative with its own factory at Umsning in Ri-Bhoi makes organic tea, and the state's Tea Development Centre sells under the Meg Tea name. One overview puts the area at nearly 2,000 hectares and output at around half a million kilograms a year.

The best-known garden abroad is Lakyrsiew, near Shillong, started by the Dutch journalist Geert Linnebank and his Khasi wife Nayantara. They began developing the garden around 2000 and planted the first bushes in 2002.
